nodes.text: Emperor Alexander I traveled in Europe with Don Cossack Platov, who disliked excessive fascination with foreign things.
The English tried to impress the sovereign with their manufactures and inventions to distract him from Russian ones.
Platov was skeptical of foreign inventions and proud of Russian craftsmen.
The English showed the sovereign a steel flea with a winding mechanism—a clockwork curiosity—that amazed him.
Platov showed a Russian inscription on a rifle screwdriver and thereby embarrassed the English.
Emperor Nicholas I, after Alexander's death, found the same clockwork flea and became interested in it.
Platov tasked the Tula masters with studying and possibly surpassing the English work on the flea.
The Tula masters worked in secret to produce something remarkable in reply to the English.
Platov sent one of them, the cross-eyed Lefty, with the flea to St. Petersburg to present the work to the sovereign.
Lefty shod the flea with real horseshoes and forged the nails himself—the secret of their craft.
The sovereign praised Russian masters and their work despite initial wonder at foreign inventions.
Lefty refused to stay in England and returned to Russia, faithful to his homeland and faith.
Lefty had plain learning from religious books, not from arithmetic.
The English marveled at Russian faith and customs; Lefty explained his devotion to homeland and religion.
Lefty was a skilled craftsman without formal schooling and knew no arithmetic.
Lefty and the English drank together during the voyage and kept wagers, staying even in the contest.
Lefty fell gravely ill and died after harsh trials in England.
Lefty warned that the English clean their rifles poorly, which could cause problems in war.
Russia did not heed Lefty's warning in time, affecting the outcome of the Crimean War.
The legend of Lefty reflects the spirit of the age and honors folk craft and loyalty to the homeland.
Machines and technology changed craftsmanship, diminishing the value of unique mastery like Lefty's.
Platov disliked when the sovereign grew too interested in foreign things, believing Russians had goods no worse.
Lefty shod the flea with horseshoes, proving Russian masters' superiority over the English.
Lefty knew no arithmetic, yet his craft and loyalty mattered more than formal education.
Lefty's warning about poor English rifle cleaning was not heard, leading to problems in war.
You are the first masters in all the world, and my people can do nothing against you.
nodes.author: Emperor Alexander I

nodes.text: You see, I knew best that my Russians would not deceive me.
nodes.author: Emperor Nicholas I

nodes.text: Tell the sovereign that the English clean rifles with brick: do not let ours be cleaned that way, or, God forbid war, they will not shoot.
nodes.author: Lefty
